title: How To Deal
full_review:
A cynical teen-ager renounces romance only to find herself falling for her close friend in the coming-of-age clunker "How to Deal" (New Line).

Full of lame dialogue and vanilla performances, this vacuous ode to adolescent angst, directed by Clare Kilner, rates on the fun scale just slightly above taking your cousin to the senior prom.
Pop star Mandy Moore plays Halley Martin, a stubbornly independent 17-year-old who has vowed never to fall in love -- a logical stance, taking into account the festering emotional wounds inflicted on her family by cupid's arrows. Her parents, Lydia (Allison Janney) and Len (Peter Gallagher), have recently finalized a bitter divorce. Len, a popular local DJ and platinum-card member of the midlife-crisis club, has just announced over the airwaves that he will be eloping with the radio station's much younger traffic reporter. If that weren't enough to sour Halley on storybook endings, watching her soon-to-be married sister, Ashley (Mary Catherine Garrison), and future brother-in-law plan their wedding is about as blissful as a cockfight.

Adding still more fuel to the fire, Halley's best friend, Scarlett (Alexandra Holden), has defected to the other side, cooing giddily over Steve (Dylan Baker), a sensitive jock, who responds with appropriate lovesick, cavity-caliber goofiness. Yet when Steve dies tragically during a high school soccer game, Halley is pushed further toward a radical emotional teetotalism.

The only chinks in her otherwise impervious amour armor are her feelings for Steve's buddy, Macon Forrester (Trent Ford), a rebel without a comb who gleans life lessons from "Star Wars." Times were when such an aptitude for science fiction would earn one the appellation of "geek" and get you stuffed in a locker, but Macon's Jedi charm works its magic on Halley, though she struggles to keep the relationship strictly platonic. Of course, Macon wants something more than friendship. As Halley's life unravels, Macon begins to challenge her fears of commitment, opening the melodramatic floodgates to predictable epiphanies about vulnerability and the inherent risks involved in love.

Moore is the most recent failed example of Hollywood's fascination with cross-pollinating stars of the music industry onto the big screen. Though attractive enough, so much of her performance is spent skulking and pouting that it is difficult to invest any emotion in her dilemma. When she isn't brooding she is spouting gag-inducing bromides like, "If love beats you up, let's beat it up right back."

The same holds true for Ford, who misguidedly mistakes his sotto-voce raspiness and I'm-too-cool-to-brush-the-hair-away-from-my-face grunge-gravitas for character depth.

The basic theme, that the human heart must risk being broken in order to love, is in itself truthful, but told in such an unappealing manner even wisdom sounds stale. The film's lack of narrative flow could be attributed to the fact that the script is a crude composite of two novels by Sarah Dessen, "Someone Like You" and "That Summer."

Regrettably, at times the film equates sex with love. However, to her credit, Kilner does show that sexual intimacy can have life-changing repercussions; Scarlett gets pregnant during sex with Steve and after his death must raise the child as a single mother. At least the narrative provides a positive portrayal of a teen-age girl willing to accept the responsibility of parenthood, rather than aborting her unborn baby.

Unfortunately, this puppy love story is for the dogs.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, brief sensuality, drug abuse, as well as an instance of rough language and some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
